lead: A rivet is a soft-metal pin with one head, put through matching holes and hammered so that a second head forms on the other side. Riveted joints are permanent, do not need welding skill and do not crack through a heat-affected zone, so they survive in bridges, truss gussets, aircraft skins and older boilers. Bonded joints use a layer of adhesive instead of fasteners: they spread the load over a whole area, join thin or unlike materials and add no holes. Both are designed by finding every way the joint can fail and making the weakest one strong enough.
prereq: You need tension, shear and crushing stress, and the bolt-group method of threaded fasteners and bolted joints for eccentric loads.

blocks.text: In a lap joint one plate overlaps the other. In a butt joint the plates meet edge to edge and one or two cover plates (straps) are riveted over the gap. Rows may be chain riveted (rivets in line) or zig-zag riveted (staggered).

items: Pitch p: the distance between rivet centres along a row.
Margin m: from a rivet centre to the plate edge, usually 1.5d.
Rivet hole diameter d: for plates over 8 mm, Unwin's formula d = 6√t (t in mm) gives a first size; for t = 10 mm, d ≈ 19 mm.

blocks.text: For structures, rivets of a tie bar are often arranged in a lozenge (diamond) pattern: one rivet in the first row, then two, then three. The plate loses only one hole at the first section, where it carries the full load, so the joint is efficient.

sections.h3: How a riveted joint fails, and its efficiency

blocks.text: Take one pitch length of the joint as a repeating strip. It can fail in four ways:

items: Tearing of the plate between the holes: P<sub>t</sub> = (p − d)tσ<sub>t</sub>.
Shearing of the rivets: P<sub>s</sub> = n(π/4)d²τ in single shear; in double shear (butt joint with two straps) about twice this.
Crushing of the plate or rivet: P<sub>c</sub> = n·d·t·σ<sub>c</sub>.
Tearing or shearing of the margin: prevented by keeping m ≥ 1.5d.

blocks.text: Here n is the number of rivets in one pitch length and σt, τ, σc are the permissible stresses. The joint is as strong as the least of these. Its efficiency compares that with the solid plate:
η is the efficiency (a fraction); p·t·σ<sub>t</sub> is the strength of an unpunched plate one pitch wide.

The best design makes P<sub>t</sub> equal to the smaller of P<sub>s</sub> and P<sub>c</sub>, which fixes the pitch. A rivet group under an eccentric load is analysed like a bolt group: direct shear P/n plus moment shear Pe·r/Σr², added as vectors.

An adhesive joint carries load through a thin layer of epoxy, acrylic, polyurethane or cyanoacrylate. Adhesives are strong in shear and weak in peel and cleavage, so joints are laid out as lap, strap or scarf joints that load the layer in shear.

blocks.where: τ<sub>avg</sub> is the average shear stress in the adhesive in MPa; P the load in N; b the joint width and l the overlap length in mm.

blocks.text: The shear is not uniform. The adherends stretch, so most of the load transfers near the two ends of the overlap, where the shear peaks (the shear-lag theory of Volkersen). A single lap joint also bends, adding peel stress at the ends. So doubling the overlap does not double the strength; widening the joint does.

items: Advantages: uniform load spread, no holes, joins thin and unlike materials, seals and damps.
Limits: weak in peel, creep and temperature limits, surface preparation decides strength, cannot be inspected easily.
Design rules: load in shear, avoid peel, taper the ends, keep bond lines thin and even, and use a rivet or bolt where peel cannot be avoided.

examples.question: A double-riveted zig-zag lap joint joins 10 mm plates. Rivet holes are 20 mm in diameter. Permissible stresses: tension 80 MPa, shear 60 MPa, crushing 120 MPa. Find the pitch and the efficiency.
steps: In one pitch length there are n = 2 rivets, each in single shear.
Shearing is the weaker, so make tearing equal to it: (p − 20) × 10 × 80 = 37 700 gives p = 67.1 mm; take p = 67 mm.
examples.answer: Pitch 67 mm, margin 30 mm, efficiency 70.1 %; the joint fails first by tearing of the plate (37.6 kN per pitch), just below rivet shear (37.7 kN).

examples.question: Two steel strips 25 mm wide are bonded in a single lap joint with 20 mm overlap. The epoxy's lap-shear strength is 20 MPa. With a factor of safety of 2, what load can the joint carry? Why would a 40 mm overlap not carry twice as much?
steps: With 40 mm overlap the average-stress formula would give 10 kN, but the shear peaks at the ends of the overlap and the middle carries little; the real gain is much smaller. Widening the joint to 50 mm doubles the strength reliably.
examples.answer: 5 kN at 20 mm overlap; for more load widen the joint or use a scarf joint rather than lengthening the overlap.

traps: Using p instead of p − d for tearing. The plate tears through the holes, so only p − d of each pitch is left.
Taking every rivet in double shear. Lap joints put rivets in single shear; only butt joints with two straps give double shear.
Calling the strongest mode the joint strength. The least of tearing, shearing and crushing decides it.
Treating adhesive shear as uniform. τ = P/(bl) is an average; the ends carry far more, so overlap length has diminishing returns.

quiz.q: Define pitch and margin of a riveted joint.
quiz.a: Pitch is the distance between centres of neighbouring rivets in a row. Margin is the distance from a rivet centre to the edge of the plate, usually 1.5d.

quiz.q: List the four ways a riveted joint can fail.
quiz.a: Tearing of the plate between rivets, shearing of the rivets, crushing of the plate or rivet, and tearing of the margin.

quiz.q: Why is a lozenge joint efficient for a structural tie bar?
quiz.a: The first row has only one rivet, so at the section carrying the full load the bar loses only one hole. Later rows remove more holes, but by then part of the load has already passed into the cover plates.

quiz.q: A single-riveted lap joint has 12 mm plates, 20 mm holes and 60 mm pitch. With σ<sub>t</sub> = 80, τ = 60 and σ<sub>c</sub> = 120 MPa, find the strength per pitch and the efficiency.
An adhesive lap joint 30 mm wide must carry 6 kN at an average shear of 8 MPa. Find the overlap.
Why does a single lap joint, riveted or bonded, see peel or tension at its ends?
quiz.a: The two plates are offset by their thickness, so the pull is not in line and the joint rotates to bring it into line. That rotation bends the plates and pulls the ends of the overlap apart: rivet heads are pulled and adhesive is peeled.

beyond: Not for the exam. Aircraft fuselages are still riveted, and car bodies now combine spot welds with structural adhesive (weld-bonding) for stiffness and crash strength. Self-piercing rivets and flow-drill screws join aluminium to steel where welding fails. Search for weld-bonding, self-piercing rivets and the single lap shear test (ASTM D1002).
